stem: Congress has fixed the boundaries of a national park by law. Later, a town mayor wants to cut off part of the park to build a subdivision. Under Article XII, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution, how can the park's area be reduced?
hints: Section 4 says what happens to forest lands and national parks after their limits are marked. Watch for an exception at the end of the rule.
Read the rule: national parks "shall be conserved and may not be increased nor diminished, except by ..." Find the last word.
"Diminished" means made smaller. A rule with "except" is not a total ban. Section 4 also says who fixes park limits "by law." Match the choice to that one exception.

solution.methodName: Apply the rule to the facts

steps.action: Recall Article XII, Section 4: after their limits are fixed, "such forest lands and national parks shall be conserved and may not be increased nor diminished, except by law."
Apply it to the facts: cutting off part of the park makes it smaller, so it diminishes the park.

Find the exception: the only way is "by law." Section 4 gives this job to Congress: "The Congress shall, as soon as possible, determine, by law, the specific limits of forest lands and national parks."
steps.why: An ordinance or a permit is not a law passed by Congress. And because there is an exception, the area is not frozen forever.

steps.action: The answer is only through a law.

trapNotes.Through a town council ordinance: Section 4 gives Congress, not the town council, the power to set park limits by law. An ordinance cannot shrink a national park.
trapNotes.Through a DENR Secretary's permit: A permit is not a law. The DENR manages parks but cannot change their area on its own.
trapNotes.Never, under any circumstances: Too strong. Section 4 says "except by law," so the area can change through a law.
